#7588. Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a new White House ballroom. On Aug. 31, a divided court paused a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that would have halted above-ground construction on the project. In a petition filed on Nov. 5, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to reverse the lower court’s ruling outright or to take up the case and hear oral arguments on the merits. He told the justices that their earlier ruling “has all but answered the question presented” by the dispute, and that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”

Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing. In December, the National Trust for Historic Preservation – a private nonprofit that describes itself as having “led the movement to save America’s historic places” “[f]or more than 75 years” – filed a lawsuit in federal court, seeking to block the construction until the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts could review the plans for the construction; the NCPC could approve those plans; and Congress could authorize the construction.

To support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and said that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month. Hoagland, who has “expertise in historic architecture,” claimed that the project caused “‘injuries’ to her ‘aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests’ because she finds the ‘scale,’ ‘height,’ and ‘massing’ of the government’s design distasteful.”

Senior U.S. District Judge Leon issued an order in late March that temporarily barred the construction of the ballroom above ground but allowed underground construction – of, for example, bomb shelters and bunkers – to move forward, along with any above-ground construction necessary for safety and security.

Before Leon’s ruling could go into effect, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit froze it to give that court time to consider the government’s appeal. In August, a divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld Leon’s ruling but delayed its effective date for 14 days to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court.

Writing for the majority, Judges Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia emphasized that Congress, and only Congress, has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures,” but it has not approved any money for the ballroom construction.

In her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao contended (among other things) that the trust did not have a legal right to bring a lawsuit, known as standing, to try to stop the ballroom construction.

Calling Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” the Trump administration came to the court on its interim docket on Aug. 13. Sauer asked the justices to temporarily pause Leon’s ruling, telling them that it would “halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.” He argued that the trust lacks standing to sue, because its claims rest on a member’s “dislike” for the new construction – which, it said, is not the kind of injury that would allow the lawsuit to go forward.

On Aug. 21, the day that Leon’s order was scheduled to go into effect, Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay – that is, an order that kept Leon’s order on hold (and permitted construction to continue) – to give the justices additional time to consider the government’s request.

By a vote of 5-4, the court on Aug. 31 granted the government’s application and continued the pause on Leon’s order. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the majority stressed that it was not deciding whether the project was legal. Instead, it said, the trust likely lacks standing to challenge the project at all. The harms that Hoagland alleges, the majority wrote, are not the kind of “concrete” and specific injuries required to bring a lawsuit. Moreover, the majority said, if Leon’s order were allowed to go into effect, the government would be permanently harmed – another key criterion in determining whether to grant emergency relief. Among other things, it noted, senior government officials “attest[] that constructing something approximating the height and mass of the intended above-ground ballroom is ‘crucial’ to the security of the below-ground military installation.”

Roberts dissented, in an opinion joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. In his view, the construction “is likely unlawful,” and the majority’s decision was “no victory for the separation of powers.” He contended that the trust did have standing to sue because “[a] historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as,” based on prior court precedent, “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys.”

In its Nov. 5 petition, the Trump administration argued that “the East Wing renovation is a vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” and that it has “proceeded swiftly since construction began in October 2025, in keeping with the urgency of remedying the East Wing’s obsolete and vulnerable security infrastructure, all as this President faces an onslaught of assassination attempts.” Because Leon’s order blocked the project “at the behest of a single passerby who complains that she expects to dislike its ultimate design,” Sauer wrote, his “decision is demonstrably flawed.”

Sauer acknowledged that the court’s Aug. 31 ruling came on the interim docket and therefore “only involve[d] a preliminary look at the merits and equities” of the dispute. But, he continued, in this case “[t]here is nothing further or new that this Court needs to decide after its” earlier opinion “in order to answer the question presented” by the government’s new filing – specifically, whether Leon was wrong to block “the ongoing renovation of the East Wing of the White House.” This is especially true, Sauer suggested, given the court made its Aug. 31 decision “after extensive briefing, and issue[d] detailed majority and dissenting opinions addressing” the issues in the case.

Sauer urged the court to summarily reverse Leon’s decision – that is, to reverse it without additional briefing or oral argument – or, at a minimum, grant review and hear oral arguments.

The trust’s response to the government’s petition is currently due on Dec. 7.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7587. In broad sweep, EEOC moves to abandon its pending gender identity bias lawsuits

In its motions to dismiss, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and guidance from the Office of Personnel Management.

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has requested dismissal of nearly every lawsuit it filed in the previous year alleging discrimination against a transgender worker or workers, less than one month after Acting Chair Andrea Lucas announced the agency would focus on “rolling back the Biden administration’s gender identity agenda.”

According to court filings viewed by HR Dive, EEOC last week filed motions to dismiss at least six pending lawsuits. These include cases against a Holiday Inn Express owner; the owner of a Home2 Suites by Hilton hotel in Alabama; an Illinois hog farm; a pizzeria located in Chicago O’Hare International Airport; a Wendy’s operator based in southern Illinois; and a Lush location based in California’s Bay Area.

The complaints included a range of charges, including employers’ tolerance of deadnaming, misgendering, “outing,” and harassing and invasive comments from co-workers. Multiple lawsuits alleged retaliation, with workers reporting they had been fired after coming to their supervisors with complaints about the conduct.

EEOC filed the lawsuits under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which the U.S. Supreme Court determined to include employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation in the landmark 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County, Ga. case.

In its motions to dismiss, the majority of which were filed Friday and used largely the same language, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and to guidance from the Office of Personnel Management requiring all federal employees to comply with the order.

“The EEOC’s continued litigation of the claim in this action may be inconsistent with the Order and the OPM Guidance,” the agency stated in each motion.

“This dereliction of EEOC’s duty under its legal mandate requires immediate judicial intervention,” Equal Rights Advocates, a legal group that advocates for “gender justice in workplaces,” said in a statement Tuesday on the move. “Transgender and gender non-conforming employees deserve the full protection of our civil rights laws, as established by Congress and the Supreme Court, not selective enforcement based on political whims and hastily issued executive orders.”

EEOC told HR Dive it would not comment on litigation.

#7583. Judge releases DUI suspect after reading AI-assisted police report disclosure

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock)

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

Anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

Court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

The officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”

Fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

#7582. Court appears unlikely to side with inmate in lawsuit for violation of his constitutional rights

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday appeared to side with a prison paramedic in a lawsuit brought by an inmate who contends that the paramedic’s failure to provide medical treatment violated his constitutional rights. During just over 80 minutes of oral argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, a majority of the justices seemed poised to throw out the inmate’s lawsuit, even if it wasn’t clear whether they were ready to bar such lawsuits more broadly in the future.

The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii. He says that he told Francis Nielsen, a paramedic who treated him, that his pain was severe, but he received only over-the-counter pain medication and was put in solitary detention, where he remained for more than two months without seeing a specialist or going to a hospital. When Watanabe received an X-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs. He relied on two Supreme Court cases: the court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, holding that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages; and its 1980 decision in Carlson v. Green, in which the court held that the estate of an inmate who died after having an asthma attack could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but explained that, in its view, “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Representing Nielsen, Lucas Walker told the justices on Monday that the Supreme Court “has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy.”

But Watanabe’s “claim ... also fails under a straightforward application of this Court’s Bivens framework,” Walker continued. “There are at least three” “meaningful difference[s] between his case and Carlson.” First, Watanabe had other options besides damages – such as seeking “administrative and injunctive relief.” Second, unlike the inmate in Carlson, Watanabe did not die, which “Congress could see [as] a meaningful difference.” Third and finally, there are “special factors” at play in Watanabe’s case that were not at play in Carlson, such as the Administrative Remedy Program, a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979, and federal laws enacted after the decision, such as the Prison Litigation Reform Act, a 1996 law that requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Vivek Suri, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the federal government, told the justices that, in the view of the United States, there are “three ways in which this Court could resolve the case.” “First, it could apply its existing standards and recognize that Carlson is now obsolete. Second, it could ... explicitly overrule Carlson. And, third, it could distinguish Carlson on its facts.” He “respectfully urge[d]” the court to choose one of the first two options, “either of which would abrogate Carlson, fully resolve the” divisions among the courts of appeals “that it has created, and end the severe practical problems that it creates for prison administration.”

Representing Watanabe, Joshua Wesneski reiterated that “the Court’s consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade” has been “[t]his far and no further.” “‘No further,’ he said, “means we should not extend those precedents. But ‘this far’ means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach.” “Indeed,” he suggested, “to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress’s measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society’s most vulnerable members.”

Neither Chief Justice John Roberts nor Justice Brett Kavanaugh seemed receptive to Walker’s suggestion that the court should go ahead and overrule both Bivens and Carlson.

Kavanaugh asked Walker how the court should handle the “fact ... that Congress has had 55 years since Bivens and 46 years since Carlson to do so and has not done so?” “It seems,” Kavanaugh continued, “like Congress, in fact, has left Bivens and Carlson where they stood ... and Congress has operated against that backdrop.”

Walker suggested that the Supreme Court “has not hesitated to overrule past decisions, especially those where the courts had overstepped the proper judicial role.”

In response to Walker’s assertion that overruling Bivens would “clear up the confusion and hand the accountability for all of this back to Congress, where it belongs,” Kavanaugh later asked whether “another way to provide clarity [would be] to simply say that courts should apply Bivens and Carlson but not extend them?” He compared such a scenario to what the Supreme Court has done in other areas of the law, such as with the Alien Tort Statute, “where we’ve had results or decisions under a methodology we wouldn’t use anymore, but we have not overruled the original three” causes of action under “the ATS, for example. We just haven’t extended them.”

Suri addressed this point during his time at the lectern, telling Kavanaugh that “[t]he problem ... as I see it ... is the Court’s decision” holding that “the PLRA itself gives rise to a new context,” as does “the availability of injunctive relief.” “So,” he continued, “if you’re going to honor that precedent, then this is a new context,” which would mean that “there are no viable Carlson claims anymore.”

For his part, Roberts noted that the federal government had “expressly” not asked the court to overrule Bivens, “and, of course, they have broad experience in this context. And I wonder,” he asked Walker, “if you have any insight into why or at least why shouldn’t we, on that question, defer to their expertise and experience on that question?”

Walker responded that “I think the answer is that this has been an area wrought with confusion where the lower courts have really called out for guidance.”

Roberts appeared unconvinced. “[O]n the other hand,” he countered, “it could be viewed as a cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question” to leave Bivens intact for now.

Several justices focused on whether, if a Carlson claim was not available, an inmate in Watanabe’s shoes would still have some remedy available to him. Justice Neil Gorsuch explored whether an inmate who was the victim of medical malpractice would still be able to obtain relief in a lawsuit against the United States (rather than the individual prison official) under Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 law that allows private citizens to sue the federal government for (among other things) injuries caused by a federal employee.

Gorsuch elicited from Suri that “[i]n almost all the cases that” he had “encountered, ... there is an FTCA claim brought in parallel” with the claim under Carlson – in part, Suri suggested, because the standard for prevailing is lower, qualified immunity does not apply, and “[y]ou have a defendant who’s able to pay, the United States.” Suri suggested that when an inmate does not bring both kinds of claims, it may be out of a desire to harass an individual prison official or because the inmates do not have lawyers and are instead representing themselves “and are confused about how to proceed. If this Court says there are no more Carlson claims,” he concluded, “then I think it’s more likely that they will bring FTCA claims in these cases.”

Justice Samuel Alito had a similar question, asking Suri “whether Bivens in this context provides anything ... of value that is not available based on other remedies.”

Suri responded that Carlson had rested on the idea that “the FTCA was insufficient” because it “does not provide for punitive damages.” In Bivens, he emphasized, the court faced a choice between “damages or nothing” for the plaintiff. But under the FTCA, he said, “you’re already getting damages.”

Wesneski pushed back on any suggestion that the FTCA, standing alone, would – as Kavanaugh put it – “provide some remedy in meritorious cases.” And there would be other potential problems as well, he posited: for example, he said, “we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA” under Indiana law.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett also expressed concern about what relief an inmate in a situation like Watanabe’s would be able to obtain. She first pressed Walker on the question of whether an inmate could obtain a court order instructing a prison official to do (or to refrain from doing) something, even if he could not obtain money damages for the official’s past conduct. “I want to make sure,” she said to Walker, “that, in your position, there’s no doubt that someone in a prisoner’s position like this would be able to get injunctive relief against a federal officer.”

And she later returned to a similar topic, asking Walker to “walk me through what happens in a case where a prisoner dies as a result of medical negligence and let’s say really horrific medical negligence. What recourse,” she enquired, “does that prisoner have? Is it the FTCA?”

Walker assured Barrett that, even if Carlson were overruled, claims like the one she described would generally be allowed to go forward.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to be the most likely to side with Watanabe. Sotomayor contended that, “in the Westfall Act, Congress looked at Bivens and explicitly reserved those constitutional claims the Court had recognized” – specifically, “Bivens itself for unlawful entry ... without probable cause into private citizens’ homes when there was malfeasance in doing so, and in Carlson itself, which was a ... medical malpractice claim.”

Walker resisted Sotomayor’s characterization, telling Sotomayor that, “respectfully, I don’t think the Court has ever gone so far as to say that the Westfall Act ratified Bivens or Carlson. But what the Court has said is that it does not provide any reason to extend those cases further.”

Jackson seemed to regard Watanabe’s case as, “with respect to all major indicia of sameness,” identical to Carlson. “We have the same kind of alleged violation as in Carlson,” she told Walker. “We have the same constitutional right brought under the same legal framework by the same kind of defendant who’s housed in the same kind of federal institution.”

By contrast, Justice Elena Kagan suggested that, at the very least, Watanabe’s case involves “factual differences.” In addition to the fact that the inmate in Carlson died, she noted that “there was a view that the prison officials had actively contributed to the injury, and ... that the prison officials knew exactly what was happening while it was happening.” “[A] different way of saying the same thing,” she added a few minutes later, “is that this looks like a pretty standard medical malpractice case, bad but standard, where the factual circumstances in Carlson look like something a good deal more than that.”

A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

A federal jury in Brooklyn today convicted Mansuri Manuchekhri, also known as “Mansuri Manchekhri” and “Manysher,” on four counts of an indictment charging him with conspiring to provide material support to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province (ISIS-K), conspiring to possess and possessing firearms and ammunition while unlawfully in the United States, and making false statements to federal agents. On October 30, 2026, Manuchekhri pleaded guilty to a fifth count charging immigration fraud relating to a sham marriage between the defendant and a U.S. citizen. The verdict was returned following a two-week trial. When sentenced, Manuchekhri faces up to 55 years in prison.

“Manuchekhri is a dangerous illegal alien who glorified ISIS’s violence, facilitated payments to ISIS-linked operatives, and unlawfully possessed firearms while living in the United States,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General M. Scott Proctor. “His support for a terrorist organization responsible for murder and atrocities around the world, disregard for our nation’s laws, and obvious hatred of the United States made him a grave danger to the public. Today’s verdict demonstrates that those who aid terrorists will be held fully accountable.”

“The defendant sent money to ISIS, a bloodthirsty terrorist organization, while training with assault rifles and proclaiming to his associates: ‘I am ready,’” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “But it is we who were ready, along with our law enforcement partners. The defendant’s conviction has neutralized a serious threat and shown the world that we will be unrelenting in dismantling terrorist funding networks.”

“Mansuri Manuchekhri's alleged extremist plans were disrupted by the outstanding work of the New York Joint Terrorism Force,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. of the FBI New York Field Office. “He spent years living in New York while supporting ISIS and declaring his allegiance to the group. Today, he is off the streets. Anyone who seeks to support or commit terrorism should know that justice will find you.”

As proven at trial, in June 2016, Manuchekhri traveled to the United States from Tajikistan on a non-immigrant tourist visa and unlawfully remained in the United States after his visa expired in December 2016. While in the United States, Manuchekhri collected jihadist propaganda videos that promoted violence and martyrdom and expressed his support for ISIS, praising past ISIS attacks in the United States such as the October 2017 West Side Highway truck attack that killed eight people and seriously injured many others. Manuchekhri’s ex-wife testified that he told her about the terrorist who carried out that deadly attack: “That guy is in heaven.”

From approximately December 2021 through June 2023, while residing in Brooklyn, Manuchekhri facilitated approximately $70,000 in payments to ISIS-affiliated co-conspirators in Turkey and Syria, including to an individual who was later arrested by Turkish authorities for his alleged involvement in a January 2024 terrorist attack on a church in Istanbul for which ISIS-K publicly claimed responsibility. In March 2017, Manuchekhri paid an American citizen to enter into a sham marriage with him so that he could obtain legal status in the United States. However, he failed to provide certain supporting documentation that was requested by the government, and his petition was never granted.

Within the same time frame as the money transfers, Manuchekhri possessed and used firearms and made frequent visits to shooting ranges even though he was prohibited from doing so as an alien unlawfully in the United States. In February 2022, he recorded himself firing an assault rifle at a shooting range in New Jersey and sent the video to one of the ISIS-affiliated individuals in Turkey with the message, “Thank God, I am ready, brother.” An invoice from the shooting range reflects that on Feb. 27, 2022, Manuchekhri and his friend rented a rifle port, an AK-47, and a Smith & Wesson M&P 15 tactical rifle, and purchased ammunition.

Manuchekhri also possessed firearms elsewhere. On Aug. 24, 2024, Manuchekhri sent a different roommate a video recorded from inside a moving vehicle showing his outstretched arm firing a handgun out the window along a highway.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew D. Reich and Lindsey R. Oken for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Pollack; Trial Attorney John Cella and Ryan White of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section; and Paralegal Specialist Wayne Colon.

#7578. Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

A Book Review of Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country (2026)”

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s new book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court. In his book, Justice Alito shares his thoughts about such subjects as originalism, textualism in statutory interpretation, the Catholic intellectual tradition, the role of judges in the United States and increasingly around the world, religious liberty in the United States, threats to the Constitution, and much more. Although there is a great deal else to be said, several things leapt out at me.

First, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned. Hence his vote to overrule Roe v. Wade after 49 years, Humphrey’s Executor after 91 years, or even a 128-year-old, long settled Supreme Court precedent like United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which would have ended birthright citizenship. (In saying this, I take no position myself on the birthright citizenship case – a debate I stayed out of.)

But Justice Alito is not simply an originalist. He also rejects the view of Professor James Bradley Thayer, and of Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Felix Frankfurter, William H. Rehnquist, and even at times of Justice Scalia that the Supreme Court should be judicially restrained and defer blindly to the political process. Justice Alito recognizes that judicial restraint where the Supreme Court has wrongly deferred to the political process is unconstitutional under Article III and has produced tragic results in cases like Plessy v. Ferguson, in which the court ratified Jim Crow race discrimination by the political branches of the government, or Korematsu v. United States, in which the court ratified President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s internment of over 100,000 innocent Japanese American citizens. In those cases the Supreme Court erred by not enforcing the Constitution. Yet at other times it has erred by being judicially activist as in Dred Scott v. Sanford or Lochner v. New York or Roe v. Wade. As Justice Alito teaches us, the Supreme Court should be neither judicially activist nor judicially restrained. It should uphold constitutional laws and strike down unconstitutional laws. This is what the rule of law is all about.

Justice Alito is equally and rightly skeptical of the notion that judges should be Dworkinian natural rights theorists, progressive constitutionalists like Chief Justice Earl Warren, or implementers of Catholic natural law as is argued by Harvard Law School Professor Adrian Vermeule. Indeed, Justice Alito devotes a whole chapter of his book to rejecting the idea that Supreme Court justices should implement natural law. This is because Justice Alito is profoundly aware that the American people during the 237 years from 1789 to 2026 have more knowledge and are thus wiser than is one individual Supreme Court, Supreme Court justice, or academic theorist. Although he does not say this outright, Alito appears to believe that originalist judges should be guided by the four cardinal virtues: 1) practical wisdom; 2) justice; 3) courage; and 4) temperance.

At the same time, Justice Alito is very much a Burkean. What does this mean? It calls to mind one of my favorite works of political philosophy, Friedrich Hayek’s volumes 1, 2, and 3 of Law, Legislation, and Liberty. In that masterpiece, Hayek identifies two forms of social order: planned systems of order like a firm or a military platoon, and spontaneous systems of social order like a language, the free market, or a culture of following the rule of law. No one has ever successfully planned a language, but languages have rules of grammar and a fixed meaning of words, and so a language forms what Hayek calls a spontaneous system of social order.

The Constitution and its amendments are a planned system of order, the words of which are so short and abstract that they have given rise to spontaneous systems of order around them. Thus, the freedom of speech and of the press protects thoughts in a private diary or a letter to a friend even though they are not vocal utterances or made with a printing press. Those words also protect freedom of expression in new technologies like movies, radio, television, or the internet, and they even protect expressive conduct that is not vocal at all like burning the American flag contemptuously at a protest rally.

The advantage of a spontaneous system of order like a language, the free market, or constitutional caselaw is that it harnesses the wisdom of many individuals who are always wiser than is one judge or academic theorist. But the countervailing advantage of the Constitution being a planned system of order is that if constitutional case law drifts too far away from the wonderful Novus Ordo Seclorum plan of the framers, the Supreme Court may overrule such caselaw – even after a century of it having been decided. The bottom line is that in figuring out when to follow the planned order of the Constitution or the spontaneous order of constitutional case law and precedents, a justice must further draw on the four cardinal virtues mentioned earlier – practical wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance.

More controversially, Alito argues that one factor in a good constitutional or statutory interpretation is that it produces good consequences. This is contrary to what Justice Scalia used to tell me when I was his law clerk, which is that if a text he is interpreting coming in is garbage, then the decision going out will also be garbage. Justice Scalia insisted it was not his job to make the law better. This differed from the approach which Judge Robert H. Bork, who I clerked for on the D.C. Circuit, followed. Judge Bork would not rewrite the Constitution or statutes to produce good results, but if there were two equally plausible readings of legal language, Judge Bork, like Justice Alito, would go with the one that produced the best outcomes in his view. I would do the same thing.

Nevertheless, in discussing Supreme Court precedents that he thinks were wrongly decided, Justice Alito can sometimes be too timid (in my opinion) in his criticisms. Perhaps that is because as a Supreme Court justice, he feels constrained in calling for the overruling of clearly incorrect precedents. For example, he criticizes Justice Scalia’s opinion in 2012’s United States v. Jones, in which the court held evidence should be suppressed which was obtained from illegally placing a GPS tracking device on a drug dealer’s car. But in his own dissent in that case Justice Alito failed to call for overruling the exclusionary rule cases on which that decision was based, even though his former boss, Attorney General Ed Meese, had publicly called for the overruling of the exclusionary rule in the 1980’s, and even though Congress passed a federal statute overruling it in the context of Miranda v. Arizona in 1968.

Justice Alito also complains rightly about the banning of religion from the public square, but he concedes in his book that as a justice he had failed to join a Scalia dissent, which called for the complete overruling of Flast v. Cohen, an absurd standing precedent of the Warren court which gave taxpayer standing to ACLU litigants who were offended by local government Christmas and Hannukah displays or displays of the Ten Commandments. And Justice Alito quite rightly criticizes Justice Scalia’s decision weakening the free exercise clause case in Employment Division v. Smith, but he does not call for overruling it. He should do so with pride.

The argument for originalism in constitutional interpretation is the same as the argument Justice Alito makes for textualism in statutory interpretation. Legal texts, be they constitutions, statutes, contracts, wills, or Supreme Court opinions should be given their original public meaning. A judge who interpreted a Supreme Court opinion or a contract according to natural law would be violating the fundamental norms of our legal system. Originalist justices can and should follow non-originalist precedents where not doing so would be disruptive to our legal system. I thus agree with Justice Alito that the Supreme Court should follow, for example, its dormant commerce clause precedents.

There is one final area where I and Justice Alito respectfully disagree. Readers of this site, and of Justice Alito’s book, know that we have different views on same-sex marriage and Obergefell v. Hodges. In his book, Justice Alito responds to me by pointing out, among other things, that same-sex marriage was unheard of for 40,000 years of human history.

I will only add here that 250 years ago, on July 4, 1776, nearly every country in the world had slavery, feudalism was widely practiced, there was a caste system in India, racism and religious persecutions were the norm, women’s rights were suppressed, and the public was adamantly opposed to LGTBQ+ rights. Gordon Wood, the famous historian of the American Founding argued in his Pulitzer Prize winning book, The Radicalism of the American Revolution that July 4, 1776 was the most important day in all of human history (other than the days of the birth and death of Jesus) because the Declaration of Independence launched a “New Order of the Ages,” which helped bring millennia of human inequality to an end in Western democracies.

It is true that same-sex civil marriage is a very new idea, but so too, in the historical scale of things, is the end or attempted end of slavery, feudalism, the Hindu caste system, racism, religious persecution, and sexism. I think the sudden rise of same-sex marriage stems from the same American Revolution that began 250 years ago on July 4, 1776.

In any event, Justice Alito is to be commended for writing an exceptionally intellectual and provocative new book. The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

#7577. Iranian Intelligence Agent Sentenced to Over 27 Years in Prison for Foiled Plot to Assassinate U.S. Government Officials

Earlier today, in federal court in Brooklyn, Asif Merchant, 48, of Pakistan, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Eric R. Komitee to 330 months in prison for attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire. Merchant is a trained operative of the Iranian government’s global terrorist force, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Merchant was convicted by a federal jury in March 2026 of traveling to the United States to arrange for political assassinations on American soil.

“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”

“The IRGC sent Merchant to avenge the strike on their terrorist commander, Qasem Soleimani,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Thanks to exceptional investigative and prosecutorial work by our federal law enforcement professionals, the plot failed.  The stiff sentence Merchant has now received should stand as a stark warning — if you come to America on behalf of a foreign power to commit terrorist acts, we will find you and lock you away.”

“Today’s sentence ensures that Asif Merchant never again has the opportunity to plan an evil attack on America,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Iran, its proxies, and its terrorist assets near and far should recognize this case as an example of U.S. law enforcement’s strength. If you plan an attack on our democracy, on our elected officials, on our people, we will stop you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law.”

“The sentencing of Asif Merchant is a victory of the FBI’s mission to secure the homeland,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. of the FBI New York Field Office. “Merchant's plot against a prominent critic of the Iranian regime posed a serious threat to public safety and our national security.  Today's sentence demonstrates that anyone who seeks to use violence or intimidation to silence dissent will face justice.  The FBI Joint Terrorism Task force will continue to work tirelessly to root out the evils of terrorism.”

By his own admission, Merchant voluntarily joined the IRGC and became a trained intelligence asset. He then traveled to the United States and, on behalf of the IRGC, located and paid hitmen to kill U.S. government officials. Merchant believed that the ultimate target of his murder plot would be Donald J. Trump but stated that other targets could have been then-President Joe Biden and former United Nations Ambassador Nikki Haley, all of whom were American presidential candidates at the time. Merchant admitted that the murder plot was motivated by Iran’s desire to avenge the death of former IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani, who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in January 2020.

As Merchant admitted in his trial testimony, he was recruited by the IRGC in approximately 2022. At that time, Merchant began traveling to Iran on religious pilgrimages and, through a relative, was introduced to his IRGC handler, Yousef Merhardad. Beginning in approximately 2023, Merchant met with his IRGC handler approximately 15 times over the course of a year and a half in Tehran, the capital of Iran. During those meetings, the IRGC handler trained Merchant on counterintelligence measures and tasked Merchant to travel to the United States to orchestrate a plot to assassinate U.S. government officials. Merchant was instructed that the hitmen he hired should be criminals or Mafia members and that they should carry out the assassination at a political rally in the United States. Merchant testified at trial that he believed the ultimate target of his plot was President Trump.

In approximately April 2024, immediately after spending a week in Iran, Merchant flew to the United States to carry out his plot. Once in the United States, Merchant contacted an acquaintance to assist him with his assassination scheme. Instead, the acquaintance reported Merchant to the FBI and served as an informant. In a video recording introduced at trial, Merchant methodically described a portion of his plot to the informant and mapped out the murder of a politician at a political rally. Merchant then reached out to purported hitmen who were actually undercover FBI agents. Merchant met three times with the purported hitmen and explained to them that he was working with people overseas and wanted to hire them to kill a politician. Merchant then paid the purported hitmen $5,000 as an initial payment for the murder plot, which Merchant obtained with the assistance of overseas relatives. After hiring the hitmen, Merchant was arrested in Richmond, Texas, on July 12, 2026, as he was about to go to the airport to leave the United States.

Evidence obtained from Merchant’s laptop, cellphones, and social media accounts showed his focus on the 2024 presidential election and President Trump. Materials introduced at trial included Merchant’s internet searches related to campaign rallies and a search using Google Maps for the location of a Trump rally in New Jersey. Merchant’s social media accounts included posts praising Soleimani and targeting President Trump and the United States.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sara K. Winik Nina C. Gupta and Gilbert M. Rein for the Eastern District of New York are in charge of the prosecution with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Magdalena St. Surin and Deputy Chief Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7576. Trump order tightens White House grip on Fed, SEC

Under the order, independent agencies must submit for review “significant” regulations to a unit within the Office of Management and Budget, and OMB Director Russ Vought has power over agency budgets.

Agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Federal Trade Commission – which Congress established as independent from the White House – would also be affected by the order.

The carve-out for the Fed on monetary policy “seems directed toward preventing a negative market reaction to the order,” said Jeff Naimon, a Washington, D.C.-based partner at law firm Orrick.

The agencies also have to employ a White House liaison, and consult regularly on policy and priorities with the OMB, the White House Domestic Policy Council and the White House National Economic Council, according to the order.  The OMB will “adjust so-called independent agencies’ apportionments to ensure tax dollars are spent wisely,” according to a fact sheet that accompanied the executive order.

“These regulatory agencies currently exercise substantial executive authority without sufficient accountability to the President, and through him, to the American people,” the order said. “Moreover, these regulatory agencies have been permitted to promulgate significant regulations without review by the President.”

The move to expand Trump’s authority is the latest by an administration that’s sought to concentrate power under the executive branch. It also reflects the influence of Vought, one of the architects of conservative blueprint Project 2025, and broadens his supervisory powers. In addition to leading OMB, Vought also is acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

“For the Federal Government to be truly accountable to the American people, officials who wield vast executive power must be supervised and controlled by the people’s elected President,” the order continued.

Naimon noted there was strong coordination between independent agencies and the White House during Trump’s prior administration, but the executive order would now require that coordination.

Legal challenges to the order are “almost certain,” Kathryn Judge, a Columbia University professor of law, said in an email.

The outcome of any litigation is less clear, however, since the judiciary has embraced a more unitary view of the executive branch and a more expansive view of executive authority, she added.

The order “represents the largest single assertion over executive power over the administrative state that I can recall, not only in my lifetime but through history,” Peter Conti-Brown, a professor of financial regulation at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said in an email. “Some aspects of this control represent departures from long-standing norms. Others are in apparent contravention of statute and will be challenged legally.”

“How much of the modern independent regulatory system survives the Trump Administration’s efforts at consolidation is anyone’s guess,” Conti-Brown said, noting that the Supreme Court has repeatedly expressed skepticism of independent agencies. SCOTUS did, however, uphold the funding structure of the CFPB.

Banks may welcome the development in the near term, since the Trump administration is widely expected to usher in an era of reduced regulatory burden. But “those shifts would be far less enduring than if implemented in other ways,” Judge said.

“Longer term, the result may be a whipsaw in regulatory and supervisory expectations,” she said. “That will make it harder for banks to make operational and other decisions that are core to their business.”

#7573. A White House ballroom petition and border wall backlash

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court Building is closed today for Veterans Day. In recognition of that, this is an abridged edition of SCOTUStoday.

The Trump administration has brought the battle over construction of a new White House ballroom back to the Supreme Court. In a petition for review filed last week but made public on Monday, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.” For more on the petition, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

On Friday, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7568. Eleven new relists in search of four votes

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

First, some old business. The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser. After three relists, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown finally got the nod. The court will decide when bankruptcy courts can refuse to enforce arbitration agreements in suits alleging violations of the automatic stay. But two-time relist Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia struck out: The court denied without comment the petition brought by Roberto Clemente’s family over Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image, which raised questions about takings of intangible property and Puerto Rico’s sovereign immunity.

After a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 new relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week. Several come in pairs or trios, and the federal government – the court’s most successful repeat litigant – advocates review in three of them.

The government seeks asylum – from the D.C. Circuit

The most consequential new relist this week may be Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. On his first day back in office, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10888, which suspended the entry of aliens “engaged in the invasion across the southern border” and barred those who violate the suspension from invoking provisions of the immigration laws that would let them stay, including asylum.

Three nonprofits and 13 individuals sued. The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States. It held unlawful the proclamation’s restrictions on asylum and other statutory protections, as well as its authorization of removal procedures outside those established by Congress, and issued a classwide injunction. A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit narrowed the class definition, but affirmed. It reasoned that although asylum is discretionary, the executive cannot categorically deny covered migrants access to asylum by proclamation and informal guidance rather than through the procedures Congress prescribed. Judge Justin Walker dissented in relevant part.

The solicitor general’s petition argues that asylum is discretionary and that the president may categorically deny it to those covered by the proclamation. Requiring the government to accept applications it has already decided to reject, the government contends, serves no purpose. It also challenges the classwide injunction and the breadth of the certified class. The government argues that the ruling threatens to revive chaos at the border. Iowa and 21 other states support the petition, arguing that the decision undermines the federal duty to protect the states against invasion.

The respondents’ brief in opposition argues that Congress expressly gave noncitizens physically present in the United States the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered, and that the president cannot eliminate that right by proclamation. They emphasize the absence of a circuit split and dispute the government’s claims that the policy was responsible for reducing border crossings. They call the remedial issues fact-bound and say the government overstates the border crisis, noting that apprehensions had already fallen more than 90% from their peak before the proclamation.

The D.C. Circuit’s mandate is stayed, leaving the asylum restrictions in place for now. The absence of a split weighs against review, but the invalidation of a major administration policy could well persuade the justices to take another trip to the border. Will the court resolve this case quickly or let it sit for a while as it decides what to do, as it has in other high-profile cases?

Our first group of cases asks whether Washington may regulate private companies that run federal immigration detention centers. In GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, a class of detainees and the state sued GEO, which operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma under a federal contract, for not paying Washington’s minimum wage to detainees in a voluntary work program for which ICE reimburses $1 a day. GEO argues it’s not a conventional labor relationship, but just an effort to prevent the detainees from becoming restless from idleness. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit certified the question to the Washington Supreme Court, which held that the state minimum-wage law applied to the detained workers. A divided panel of the 9th Circuit then rejected GEO’s supremacy clause defenses, leaving GEO with a judgment it puts at about $37 million. Seven judges voted to rehear the case en banc, and six joined dissents, arguing that (among other things) the state law “interferes with federal immigration-detention policy” and thus directly regulates the federal government.

GEO argues that Washington cannot regulate a federal detention program through a contractor while exempting its own detainees from the wage law. Washington and the detainees respond that the law applies equally to every private detention contractor, whether it works for a city, the state or the federal government, and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit applies the same test as the 9th. The detainees also note that ICE has since revised its detention standards, which they say limits the decision’s future impact.

In a court-invited amicus brief, the U.S. solicitor general recommends granting review. The government argues that the law discriminates against the federal government, because Washington exempts its own facilities while barring itself from contracting with private ones, and that federal statutes leave detainee pay to the Secretary of Homeland Security. It also says the decision conflicts with a decision of the 3rd Circuit ruling on a New Jersey law targeting private detention contractors.

GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson challenges a 2023 Washington statute regulating private civil detention facilities, which GEO says reaches its Tacoma facility alone. The district court preliminarily enjoined it, but the 9th Circuit vacated that ruling, rejecting GEO’s direct regulation and preemption claims and remanding on its discrimination claim against private contractors. GEO says Washington is micromanaging federal detention by regulating a contractor; the state says its requirements resemble those governing other civil facilities. It also points to further proceedings on remand as a reason not to intervene yet.

A grant in Nwauzor seems likely; Ferguson presents a closer question, but at minimum it seems likely to be held if Nwauzor is granted.

Two companies that went public while business was booming present a question of required disclosures in federal securities filings: How much bad news must a company reveal? Two related relists ask the justices to clarify when withholding information makes an IPO registration statement misleading under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933.

In Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, the online brokerage rode the GameStop meme-stock frenzy and Dogecoin boom into its July 2021 IPO. Robinhood warned that trading might decline and provided an estimate of second-quarter revenue, but investors say it withheld information showing that trading and other business metrics were already declining. A district court dismissed their claims, but a divided panel of the 9th Circuit revived them. Robinhood’s petition argues that merely omitting material information cannot create liability unless the omission makes an affirmative statement misleading or violates a specific disclosure requirement. The investors respond that the company’s disclosures presented a misleading picture of its performance. The U.S. solicitor general, invited to weigh in, recommends granting review on the Section 11 misleading-omissions question, but not on a separate question concerning disclosures of known trends under Item 303 of Regulation S-K (which the agency is reviewing).

In ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, a webinar-platform provider prospered as businesses moved online during the pandemic. Investors allege that the company knew before the IPO that many pandemic-era customers did not intend to renew. An unpublished 9th Circuit memorandum revived the suit. ON24 asks whether describing an unmaterialized risk as hypothetical is misleading, alleging a split with the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd and 10th Circuits, and raises two questions that overlap with Robinhood’s. ON24 argues that the court improperly required it to predict future customer cancellations; the investors respond that “the warned-of risk was already materializing.” ON24 also asks the justices either to grant its petition or hold it for Robinhood. Leadersel Innotech answers that the 9th Circuit decision is non-precedential and that the panel found the risk had already begun to materialize.

With the solicitor general supporting review in Robinhood, a grant there looks plausible. Whether ON24 gets invited along is less certain. It seems a likelier hold.

It’s not every week that the Taliban is a respondent in the Supreme Court. That said, it has not responded, leaving an Afghan diplomat filing an amicus brief to oppose review – not on the Taliban’s behalf, but on behalf of the Afghan people.

When the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, the Treasury Department blocked billions of dollars that Da Afghanistan Bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Victims holding judgments against the Taliban sought to execute on the funds under Section 201(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which makes the blocked assets of a terrorist party and its “agency or instrumentality” subject to execution.

A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover. It held that an entity’s status as a terrorist organization’s instrumentality must be determined when its assets were blocked, before the Taliban installed its officials at the bank. Separately, the panel rejected other plaintiffs’ attempt at prejudgment attachment, holding that Da Afghanistan Bank enjoys sovereign immunity as the central bank of Afghanistan, which the executive continues to recognize as a foreign state. Judge Richard Sullivan dissented.

In Havlish v. The Taliban, judgment holders challenge the blocking-date rule, alleging a conflict between the 2nd Circuit and the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 9th and 11th Circuits. They are backed by Iowa and 30 other states.

In Owens v. The Taliban, plaintiffs who lacked judgments when the district court ruled say the 2nd Circuit is the first court of appeals to require courts to defer to the executive on “foreign state” status, and thus “breaks with th[e] consensus” positions of the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd, and 6th Circuits. Ashton v. The Taliban joins Owens in arguing that courts should not defer to the executive branch in determining whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, and seeks a GVR in light of this year’s decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A.

As noted, no respondent has appeared. The only opposition is an amicus brief jointly filed in the three cases by Naseer Faiq, chargé d’affaires of Afghanistan’s mission to the United Nations, who says no one is currently authorized to appear for Afghanistan in U.S. courts. He argues that the facts are unlikely to recur, that there is no circuit split, and that the immunity issue affects only the petitioners’ priority among creditors. The Havlish petitioners have sought leave to respond, arguing that the legal question is likely to recur in terrorism litigation and does indeed implicate a circuit split.

At the very least, the court will need more time to figure out what to do when the respondent seems unwilling to appear to defend the cases.

How many places can a state declare off-limits to firearms before the Second Amendment right to carry in public becomes largely theoretical? That’s the question in Novotny v. Moore, a challenge to Maryland’s extensive restrictions on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”

Maryland prohibits licensed gun owners from carrying firearms in numerous locations, including public transportation, parks and forests, healthcare facilities, museums, stadiums, casinos, public demonstrations, and establishments serving alcohol. I thought this was America! A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld those restrictions, finding historical support for them under the Supreme Court’s decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Judge G. Steven Agee dissented as to many of the restrictions, warning that the majority had stretched the sensitive-places exception too far. The panel separately struck down Maryland’s presumptive ban on carrying firearms on private property open to the public.(After this year’s decision in Wolford v. Lopez, which struck down Hawaii’s similar private-property rule, Maryland dropped its own cert petition seeking review of that ruling.)

The gun owners’ petition argues that historical restrictions on carrying firearms in sensitive places were generally limited to locations where the government provides security, not ordinary places where people gather. Maryland responds that historical regulations support restrictions at crowded places and locations serving vulnerable populations, and contends that review is unnecessary because the lower courts largely agree on the governing principles.

Invoking Wolford, the petitioners ask the justices to grant review or at least send the case back for reconsideration. Whether the court is ready to take on the sensitive-places doctrine so soon after Wolford remains to be seen. But reconsideration under Wolford seems like a real possibility.

In Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, the Commission fined Sprint $12.2 million and T-Mobile $80.1 million for failing to adequately safeguard customers’ location information shared with third-party aggregators, including by continuing to disclose the information after learning of significant security vulnerabilities. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the penalties, concluding that information about a cellphone’s location – even when no call is underway – qualifies as confidential “customer proprietary network information” under the Communications Act.

The carriers’ petition argues that the statute protects only call-location information, not all device-location data. They also contend that the FCC circumvented a statutory penalty cap by treating separate relationships with third-party companies as multiple “continuing violations,” and that the D.C. Circuit improperly deferred to the agency’s interpretation despite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. But the carriers’ principal request is narrower: They ask the justices to send the case back in light of this year’s decision in FCC v. AT&T, which held that an FCC forfeiture order does not itself compel payment. That opinion, the carriers say, rested on a key government concession: A company can refuse to pay and contest the penalty in a subsequent enforcement proceeding with a jury. Sprint and T-Mobile say they paid under protest because the FCC’s orders demanded payment and existing precedent left them little choice. The government responds that the carriers always had the option not to pay, that they failed to preserve their claim of being misled, and that AT&T provides no reason for reconsideration. The carriers disagree.

A remand remains possible, although the government notes that the court rejected a comparable request from Verizon. For now, Sprint and T-Mobile are hoping the justices will take their call.

How long can a “hot pursuit” stay hot after police lose sight of the suspect? That’s the question in City of North Las Vegas v. Jones, a case arising from a search for a suspected domestic abuser that ended with police entering a stranger’s backyard and shooting two dogs. The suspect was never found.

After officers saw a man flee over a backyard wall, the officers stated that they established a neighborhood perimeter rather than pursuing him on foot. A K-9 officer arrived about 18 minutes later, and during the ensuing search, his police dog alerted them toward a walled backyard. An officer climbed in without a warrant. Three pit bulls emerged, two of which attacked the police dog and were shot. The dogs’ owners, Genoa Jones and Cornell Tinsley, sued. The district court granted the officers qualified immunity, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed on the warrantless-entry claim, holding that the officers had not been in immediate and continuous pursuit and that circuit precedent clearly established the search’s illegality. It left intact qualified immunity for shooting the dogs. Eight judges dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc.

The city’s petition argues that the officers never abandoned the pursuit: They say they established a perimeter and used a police dog to locate a potentially dangerous suspect. Even if the search was unlawful, the city argues, no sufficiently specific precedent clearly established that fact. It also asks the justices to hold that only Supreme Court decisions – not lower-court precedent – can clearly establish law for qualified-immunity purposes. The homeowners respond that the officers never actually established a perimeter or chased the suspect and instead just conducted a neighborhood-wide search without knowing his whereabouts.

The eight dissenting judges may help keep the petition warm. But the court closely reviews many petitions in cases where police are denied qualified immunity, and unless the error was clear enough to warrant summary reversal, the justices may let this pursuit go cold – perhaps with a dissent from denial of cert.

The court has enough to chew on that it seems likely to take a while to finish processing this week’s new offerings. As for me, I’ll be watching Monday’s orders to find out how much of this I get to reuse.

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause allows a state to reclassify federal immigration detainees participating in a federal work program as employees and thereby impose its state minimum-wage law just because a private contractor provides detention services at the federal facility where the detainees are housed.

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by failing to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider material, without an inquiry into whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading; and (2) whether an issuer violates Item 303 – and thus Section 11(a)’s required-statements prong – by failing to disclose and quantify interim financial data before quarterly reporting deadlines.

Issue: Whether Maryland’s numerous prohibitions on carrying firearms in many places frequented by the general public violate the Second and 14th Amendments.

City of North Las Vegas, Nevada v. Jones, 25-1355

Issues: (1) Whether officers’ warrantless search of a backyard in close proximity to the domestic violence victim’s residence was a lawful “hot pursuit” when the suspect’s trail was temporarily lost within the perimeter for approximately 18 minutes but recovered through immediate and continuous police efforts; (2) whether, even if the search did not qualify as a “hot pursuit,” the officers were entitled to qualified immunity because no “clearly established law” was violated; and (3) whether, in the interest of avoiding the perpetual flood of federal court qualified immunity litigation, the court should decide that clearly established law means only the decisions of the Supreme Court, and not lower court decisions, which fail to provide police departments with meaningful guidance because they are highly fact-determinative and subject to numerous differing and often contradictory judicial interpretations.

ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, 25-1376

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by describing unmaterialized risks as hypothetical; (2) whether an issuer violates Section 11(a)’s misleading-omissions prong whenever it omits information related to a disclosed fact regardless of whether the omission renders an affirmative statement misleading; and (3) whether an issuer violates Item 303 of Regulation S-K – and thus the prong of Section 11(a) prohibiting the omission of required statements – by failing to disclose immaterial facts as “known trends or uncertainties” that are reasonably likely to have a material impact on financial results.

Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, 25-1422

Issues: (1) Whether this court should grant, vacate, and remand in light of FCC v. AT&T, Inc. and the government’s concessions in that case; (2) whether “location” customer proprietary network information under 47 U.S.C. § 222 refers only to call-location information, not other formation about the location of a mobile device; and (3) whether the number of “continuing violations” arising from a single failure to act under 47 U.S.C. § 503(b) is a legal question for courts to decide, without deferring to the Federal Communications Commission’s conclusion.

Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes a government speech.

Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, whether the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation.

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

#7567. Justice Department Surpasses $1B In Awards Under Reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Justice Department announced today that it has awarded more than $1 billion in compassionate compensation to newly eligible claimants under the recently reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA).

RECA was originally enacted in 1990 as a non-adversarial alternative to litigation for individuals who contracted certain illnesses following exposure to radiation as a result of the United States’ atmospheric nuclear testing program and uranium ore processing operations during the Cold War. The law sunset in 2024 and the Department ceased accepting new claims. In 2025, as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Congress reauthorized the law and expanded the scope of the RECA’s coverage.

“We are proud that the Civil Division has delivered more than $1 billion in compensation to Americans under the reauthorized Radiation Exposure Compensation Act. Congress determined that these individuals deserve compensation, and the Civil Division is honored to help ensure they receive the benefits that Congress provided,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Jonathan Guynn of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This extraordinary law provides partial restitution to individuals and their families who were subject to increased risk of disease to serve the national security interests of the United States. I am especially proud of the extraordinary work of our team in administering this program efficiently and expeditiously, while remaining faithful to the law. This achievement reflects the dedication and professionalism of the Division’s attorneys and staff who made it possible, in addition to this law’s supporters in Congress who continue to make valuable contributions and provide support.”

In its present form, RECA provides lump sum compensation awards to individuals who contracted specified diseases in four defined populations: “downwinders,” who are individuals who developed certain cancers after presumed exposure to radiation released during the atmospheric nuclear tests conducted within the United States between 1945 and 1962; “onsite participants” who participated in a test involving the atmospheric detonation of a nuclear device and later contracted a compensable disease; “uranium workers” who were employed in certain uranium extraction and processing occupations between 1942 and 1990; and individuals who developed a covered illness after living, working, or attending school in certain areas affected by Manhattan Project waste contamination. Compensation available under RECA ranges from $25,000 to $100,000 depending on the context of presumed exposure.

RECA Compensation has been awarded to individuals residing in every state.  Since July 4, 2025, over 67,000 claims have been filed and over 14,000 claims have been approved.  Additional information is available on the Civil Division’s RECA website, www.justice.gov/civil/reca.

#7565. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.
